courses.name: Language, Freedom and Linguistic Human Rights in Africa
The Literary Lives of African Women

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions This course examines the dynamics of multilingualism and language practices in the context of migrant populations, with a particular focus on Francophonie, Africa, and African diasporas. Through an analysis of the interactions between language, culture, and identity, we will explore how African migrants in Europe, North America, Asia, and within the African continent navigate between their native languages and the languages of their host countries. The course will address the sociolinguistic, psychological, and cultural issues associated with multilingualism, as well as the language policies that influence Francophone communities. Students will be invited to reflect on how language shapes the migratory experiences and cultural identities of African diasporas, while considering the contemporary challenges they face in a constantly evolving world. They will also have opportunities for experiential and immersive experiences across the GTA and within African diasporic communities.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - The Media of Witches This class explores how the historical and contemporary dominant media technologies and the institutional power structures they are part of influenced and continue to influence cultural perceptions and receptions of witches in the West. From the printing press’ role in the witch trials to social media covens, we’ll explore the complex history of a figure whose social stigma includes religious and political persecution, gendered violence, and, in contemporary periods, empowerment. From the fifteenth-century text, Malleus Maleficarum and Shakespeare’s Macbeth to popular shows like the Vampire Diaries , we’ll explore how dominant media technologies and power structures of the time always play a role in shaping cultural understandings and representations of the witch.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - The Book Culture of the European Fairy and Folk Tale This course explores the cultural history and representation of European fairy and folk tales in a variety of print forms. Students will study a range of tales from medieval romance, early modern broadside ballads, chapbooks, and early fairy tale collections as well as later folklore and fairytale compilations. They will examine the cultural, literary, and textual histories of such works as Le piacevoli notti, the Tale of Tales, Child’s ballads, tales of Charles Perrault and Brothers Grimm, and collections by Trevelyan, Crofton Crocker, and Andrew Lang. Throughout the course, students will be examining both the evolution of selected motifs and the relationship between that evolution and the differing print forms through which they were represented and circulated.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - Grand Theft Auto and the Culture of Video Games Since the 1997 release of Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar Games has been celebrated for its creative, technological, and commercial achievements and condemned for its sensational depictions of sex, violence, and urban criminality. Rockstar has long pursued artistic legitimacy by earnestly emulating iconic film genres while intentionally stoking the flames of controversy with provocative, often crude, attempts at social satire. But beyond credulous celebration and censorious condemnation, what is the significance of Grand Theft Auto as a cultural phenomenon? With Grand Theft Auto VI hotly anticipated in November 2026, this course offers a timely retrospective on the (in)famous game publisher and its flagship series, grounded in the theories and methods of media studies. Through scholarly readings, gameplay, film screenings, news coverage, marketing campaigns, archival materials, and hands-on research, students will critically investigate Grand Theft Auto’s enduring role in the history, industry, and culture of video games.

courses.name: Advanced Topics in Celtic Studies I

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101 - Nature Poetry of Ireland, Scotland, and Wales The natural beauty of Ireland, Scotland, and Wales has been celebrated by poets for centuries. This seminar will offer a chronological survey of the verse inspired by these places from early medieval poems to the work of contemporary poets. Our primary aim will be to explore the wide range of responses that the distinctive climates of the Celtic nations has produced. This approach will open a comparative perspective on the poetic traditions of these places, and will allow us to consider the ethical, intellectual, and spiritual dimensions of these traditions as well. While we will focus primarily on poetry written from within Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, we will also discuss the work of English and American poets who have written about these nations and their regions. Poets featuring in this seminar may, therefore, include: Burns, Wordsworth, Hopkins, Yeats, Dylan Thomas, Allen Ginsberg, Seamus Heaney, and Kathleen Jamie. Although any experience with poetry in an academic context will be an asset, no prior coursework is required.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions Gaza and the Regional War: Genocide, Imperialism, and Resistance in the Middle East Examines the political catastrophes of the twenty-first century: the ongoing genocide in Gaza, and its reverberations across Palestine and the broader Middle East. Beginning with the events of October 7, 2023, and moving through the subsequent Israeli military campaigns in Gaza and the West Bank, the war in Lebanon and Iran, confrontations with Yemen, the transformation of Syria, and the deepening entanglements of Gulf states, the course asks: what does this moment demand of us as scholars, students, and human beings?

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions Mad Studies, Abolition, and Carceral Logics Introduces students to Mad Studies as a field grounded in the lived experiences, histories, and cultural production of Mad people, survivors of psychiatry, and neurodivergent communities. Anchored in abolitionist praxis, the course examines the interlocking operations of the Medical Industrial Complex and the Prison Industrial Complex, and how carceral logics shape systems of care, containment, and psychiatric governance. Explores disability and madness as sites of both oppression and world-building.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The DTS305 special topics course for the 26-27 year is "Home". Where is home? Is it a house with walls and windows, a country with borders and flags, a language spoken effortlessly, or a feeling that flickers when we recognize ourselves in others? In a political moment marked by migration, displacement, and rising levels of nationalism, the meaning of home feels at once intimate and contested. This course, in response, explores how the home has come to be imagined among citizens and strangers, families and foreigners, insiders and outsiders. Readings will include social theorists interested in how the language of domestic life travels into national and imperial projects as well as histories of homes built, defended, lost, and remade. In asking what it means to be at home, this course examines the architecture of belonging itself.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The DTS402 advanced topics course for the 26-27 year is "Borders". In the era of rapid and massive transnational flows of commodities and capital, people’s mobility is forcefully constrained by heavily securitized borders. This course focuses on borders and their adjacent cities to examine current processes constituting neoliberal capitalism. Borders index geopolitical, symbolic, and legal boundaries. They simultaneously function as sites for gendering and racializing bodies and are a stage for violent encounters. Border cities are places where different forms of Otherness coalesce. By examining borders and processes of boundary-making in the Americas, Europe, and the Middle East, this course explores the ways race, class, gender, sexuality, and nationality intersect in shaping how people live (and die) along borders. While exploring ‘dehumanization’ as a mechanism that normalizes violence against Others, we will also discuss attempts to re-imagine a world without borders.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The DTS403 advanced topics course for the 26-27 year is "Palestine". This course focuses on the lived experience of Palestinians across displacement, occupation, and diaspora, with particular attention to the material and symbolic meanings of land. Through literature, history, transnational theory, and oral testimony, it explores how belonging, rootedness, and identity are shaped by loss and by the ongoing struggle to remain connected to Palestine as a material place. Discussions will grapple with terms such as displacement, exile, and refugeehood, asking how each carries a different political weight, how they are defined within a settler-colonial reality, and how these meanings shape the question of the right of return for Palestinians. We will also examine how these conditions produce transnational networks of solidarity that invite us to (re)consider what it means to engage in liberation politics from a distance. Readings will foreground voices from Palestine and the Palestinian diaspora, drawing on the work of scholars and writers such as Rashid Khalidi, Salim Tamari, Sherene Saikaly, Lila Abu-Lughod, Ghassan Kanafani, Adania Shibli, among others.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The DTS404 advanced topics course for the 26-27 year is "Refugees". This seminar explores how “the refugee” is produced, understood, and experienced across contemporary societies. Rather than approaching this through a single lens—such as policy, public opinion, or personal narrative—the course examines how these domains intersect, clash, and inform one another. Through sustained engagement with texts that reveal tensions between governance, public representations, and lived realities, students will examine how refugees’ lives are shaped by social and institutional forces, and how refugees navigate and respond to these conditions. Emphasis is placed on close, critical reading and analysis, asking how different forms of knowledge about refugees are created, how authority and voice are distributed, and how "refugeeness" comes to be known, debated, and lived.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101: Cultural Diplomacy for a Changing World This advanced undergraduate course critically examines the theory and practice of cultural diplomacy in the contemporary global system. Focusing primarily on the past three decades since the end of the Cold War, the course interrogates the dominance of the “soft power” paradigm and evaluates its explanatory power in an era of shifting geopolitical, technological, and cultural dynamics. Students will explore how cultural diplomacy has been practiced through a range of platforms and media, including exhibitions, world fairs, museums, music, sports, and other forms of cultural exchange. In addition to analyzing the longer-standing strategies of nation-states in North America and Europe, the course examines the growing role of new and emerging actors—most notably China—in reshaping the field. A key theme of the course is a critical assessment of the field’s methodological nationalism. Students will investigate how cultural diplomacy operates beyond the state, paying particular attention to the roles of institutions, cities, non-state organizations, and individual cultural actors in an increasingly interconnected world. By situating cultural diplomacy within broader debates about global order, power, and identity, the course asks how the concept and practice of cultural diplomacy must evolve in response to contemporary global transformations. The course combines theoretical analysis with experiential learning. Students will participate in a Cultural Diplomacy Academy organized by the North American Cultural Diplomacy Academy, engage in museum visits, and interact with students in a parallel course at Western University. These activities are designed to connect scholarly perspectives with real-world practices and professional networks in the field of cultural diplomacy LEC0201: The Global Art Market: Practical Applications This seminar teaches students the practical skills required to achieve success as a professional in today’s dynamic art market. Students will directly engage with the local and global art world, learn how to prepare for an art fair, navigate the complexities of a public art project, and conduct studio visits with established artists.

This advanced undergraduate course critically examines the theory and practice of cultural diplomacy in the contemporary global system. Focusing primarily on the past three decades since the end of the Cold War, the course interrogates the dominance of the “soft power” paradigm and evaluates its explanatory power in an era of shifting geopolitical, technological, and cultural dynamics. 

Students will explore how cultural diplomacy has been practiced through a range of platforms and media, including exhibitions, world fairs, museums, music, sports, and other forms of cultural exchange. In addition to analyzing the longer-standing strategies of nation-states in North America and Europe, the course examines the growing role of new and emerging actors—most notably China—in reshaping the field. 

A key theme of the course is a critical assessment of the field’s methodological nationalism. Students will investigate how cultural diplomacy operates beyond the state, paying particular attention to the roles of institutions, cities, non-state organizations, and individual cultural actors in an increasingly interconnected world. By situating cultural diplomacy within broader debates about global order, power, and identity, the course asks how the concept and practice of cultural diplomacy must evolve in response to contemporary global transformations. 

The course combines theoretical analysis with experiential learning. Students will participate in a Cultural Diplomacy Academy organized by the North American Cultural Diplomacy Academy, engage in museum visits, and interact with students in a parallel course at Western University. These activities are designed to connect scholarly perspectives with real-world practices and professional networks in the field of cultural diplomacy

 

LEC0201: The Global Art Market: Practical Applications 

This seminar teaches students the practical skills required to achieve success as a professional in today’s dynamic art market. Students will directly engage with the local and global art world, learn how to prepare for an art fair, navigate the complexities of a public art project, and conduct studio visits with established artists.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions This course is taught in English. Are you curious about German culture? What comes to your mind when you think of things German? Beer and sausages, high-performance cars, the Black Forest, or a mania for efficiency? This course moves beyond these cultural stereotypes and offers a kaleidoscopic view of German culture in its varied manifestations, be it in the form of cultural artifacts, great works of literature, family histories, or big ideas. We will explore world-shaping ideas and inventions from the Reformation and the Gutenberg Press to Bauhaus and modern industrial design, the connection between the Grimm Brothers’ fairy tales and their nation-building efforts, German fantasies about Indigenous North America and the longing for untouched nature, and personal narratives that grapple with the Nazi past and divided Germany. Ideal for students from across the disciplines, the course invites you to think critically about what constitutes German culture while expanding your cross-cultural understanding and global perspective. (No knowledge of German required.)

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions This course is taught in English. Open to all students. Germany’s recent World Cup defeat sent shockwaves through the nation — politicians weighed in, former athletes spoke out, and players with migrant backgrounds faced racist attacks online. Why does football hit so hard? The seminar explores football’s manifold impact on German society — shaping art, politics, and national memory from 1945 to today. We’ll dive into gender, class, fandom, racism, nationalism, and internationalism through the lens of the “people’s game.”

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The course is taught in German. GER350H GERMAN VISUAL CULTURES: Dialogue and Cultural Identity in German Cinema Why do we look at screens to understand who we are? GER350 is a cinematic journey through German history, identity, and modern culture. This course combines film analysis with a dynamic, discussion-driven format: every week features a curated 2-hour screening lab followed by an interactive seminar centered around critical dialogue and debate. We will break down iconic cinematography—from post-war rubble realities to the high-octane rhythms of 1990s Berlin techno-culture, and the modern transnational identities of the Berlin School. We will explore formal visual aesthetics, engage in deep thematic discussions, and examine how cinema acts as a powerful mirror for cultural discourse.

Why do we look at screens to understand who we are? GER350 is a cinematic journey through German history, identity, and modern culture. This course combines film analysis with a dynamic, discussion-driven format: every week features a curated 2-hour screening lab followed by an interactive seminar centered around critical dialogue and debate. We will break down iconic cinematography—from post-war rubble realities to the high-octane rhythms of 1990s Berlin techno-culture, and the modern transnational identities of the Berlin School. We will explore formal visual aesthetics, engage in deep thematic discussions, and examine how cinema acts as a powerful mirror for cultural discourse.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The course is taught in English. The story of modern Yiddish literature is one of resistance and creativity. This course traces the history of Yiddish literature over two hundred years of Jewish diasporic life to investigate what it means to write literature in Yiddish. Students will engage with Hasidic tales and Neo-Hasidic stories, satires and tragicomic family narratives, modernist poetry and horrifying literatures of violence. All the while, we will put Yiddish literature in conversation with world literature, locating Yiddish firmly in the constellation of international writing. All readings are in English.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions This course explores how the Internet and digital technology more broadly are affecting politics, as well as how politics is affecting the Internet. Students will consider ways in which the Internet is affecting relations between states. This can include the creation of new governance structures to regulate the Internet, as well as use of the Internet for malicious purposes and to coerce adversaries. Students will learn how the Internet is changing markets, creating new challenges for governments, businesses, and labor. The course explore how states, corporations, and users compete to control technology platforms such as Facebook, Google, and Wikipedia, which play a pivotal role in shaping the global public sphere.

notes.text: Timetable Instructions Description: This course explores the role of state size in world politics. Students will consider different ways to categorize states and analyze the ways in which power is exercised in world politics. The course explores how states have varied in size over the course of history and seeks to explain this variation. Students will consider the unique political, economic, and social advantages, disadvantages, challenges, and needs of states of varying sizes. Lastly, the course seeks to understand how and whether the size of states explains their foreign policy behaviors, economic outcomes, and domestic policies.

notes.text: Timetable Instructions This course draws upon the knowledge streams of Indigenous and Buddhist perspectives to explore wellness on the individual and system levels. Classes take place both in a classroom and the Mother Earth Learning lodge at New College. Teachings focus on relationality, interconnection to the earth, along conceptual models of attention, self and non-self. Investigate questions related to building inclusive communities amidst an increasingly divisive and complex world. The course integrates multi-modal learning modalities, including didactic lectures, hands-on experiential practices and land-based learning. This course may count towards Breadth Requirement 2: Thought, Belief, and Behaviour. If you wish to use this course towards this Breadth Category, please contact your College Registrar's Office to request for it to be manually applied.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions LEC0101:Early Islamic Architecture and Related Arts Early Islamic architecture and art emerged from a variety of sources, including Roman-Byzantine styles in Greater Syria (Al-Sham) and the Sassanian architecture and art of pre-Islamic Persia. During its formative phase, Islamic architecture and art were not limited to a single religion, period, place, or medium. Instead, they spanned multiple regions and encompassed a broad range of artistic fields, including architecture, mosaics, stucco, frescoes, ceramics, and woodwork, among others, each carrying significant spiritual, artistic, and practical meaning. This course offers a detailed study of Islamic architecture and art from its earliest period at the beginning of Islam in the 7th century through the end of the Fatimid period in 1171 AD. It seeks to develop an understanding of early Islamic architecture and art within the Muslim city in the Middle East and al-Andalucía in their broader cultural context, highlighting both their distinctive architectural, decorative, and artistic characteristics and their roots in Byzantine, Sassanian, and Arabic traditions, while examining how these elements evolved and developed their own forms in planning, architecture, and decorative techniques.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions Drugs, Poisons, and Public Policy: The Role of Pharmacology & Toxicology in Policy-Making This course will discuss the policy making process and the application of pharmacology and toxicology to the development of evidence-based policies to protect human health from exposure to drugs and chemicals, such as cannabis, opioids, carcinogens and pesticides. It will also discuss various other factors (e.g., fiscal, political) that influence policy decisions, and the importance of effective science communication. The course intends to bridge the gap between science and policy, and enhance science-based policy making and communication. Student inquiries should be directed to the course department: undergrad.pharmtox@utoronto.ca.

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions The Research Participation course (POL 395H/396H) is a 0.5 credit course for supervised participation in faculty research project. This course is offered only when a faculty member is willing and available to supervise . The interested faculty member review plans with the Undergraduate Director and then make the opportunity known to students as appropriate. The information will be posted on our website https://www.politics.utoronto.ca/undergraduate/curriculum-course-information/research-participation-courses and students can pick up an application form from the undergraduate office. POL 395H/396H is only available to students in their third year of study (i.e., who have completed at least 9.0 credits). The course is like POL 299Y in that it gives undergraduate students an opportunity to engage in research with a faculty member. notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions Students will be expected to watch asynchronous lecture videos prior to in-person tutorials. Weekly in-person Physiology in Practice classes with professors will take place on Wednesdays from 14:00 to 15:00 at Con Hall. Term tests will be held in person and on campus and will take place Mondays, Wednesdays, or Fridays from 14:00 to 15:00 (Toronto time) on scheduled dates (TBA). Lectures ~3h/week, Physiology in Practice classes 1h/week, and five (5) in-person one (1) hour tutorials per term. The lecture videos will be posted to watch asynchronously. Physiology in Practice classes, tutorials, and tests will run in-person. Delivery Instructions Approx 3 hours of online lecture recordings that can be viewed at any time. 1 hour Physiology in Practice session with the professor 2 to 3 pm at Con Hall in person 5 X 1-hour tutorials with TAs in-person throughout the term. In-person tests and exams. There are two in-person term tests, 50 minutes each generally set for Fridays, but might also be on Mondays or Wednesdays — time 2 to 3 pm. The final in-person assessment will be announced by the Faculty of Arts and Science. Please do not schedule any classes or labs during the test periods, as they will conflict with the Physiology in Practice and testing times. Conflicts will not be accommodated.

courses.name: Modern Atheism and Critique of Religion: Hegel to Nietzsche
Advanced Topics in the Philosophical Study of Religion

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Delivery Instructions While Buber’s book, I and You, is one of the most prominent philosophy books from the 20th Century; it is part of an ongoing conversation in philosophy of religion. This course will explore a series of different thinkers’ accounts of the you, exploring not only the human sociality performed by saying you to someone else, but also the nature of prayer and saying you to God. There are many basic questions: Does saying you make the you present? Is the I and You symmetrical? Can the relationship performed in language survive beyond the moment of speaking? How does the I change in addressing the you?

notes.name: Course Note
notes.text: Timetable Instructions This course traces how hip-hop grew from house parties and DJ battles in the South Bronx in the late 1970s into one of the world's dominant cultural movements. While following the historical growth of hip-hop, the course utilizes the culture as a lens to understand critical urban issues of the 20th and 21st century. The course begins with a deep dive into hip-hop's origins in New York City, then moves to a thematic examination of specific issues. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, students analyze the work of major artists, explore how cultural, economic, and social forces drive urban change, consider how hip-hop can be a tool to advance positive social policy outcomes, and deepen skills for interpreting the music.
